The problem

Your books know what you spent. They don't know where the project stands.

A general ledger records transactions: what was invoiced and what was paid out, tagged to a job or customer if someone remembered to. Running projects takes more than that. You need to know what each job should cost, what it will cost, how much revenue it has earned, and whether billing is ahead or behind.

And not every project has a customer. The warehouse addition you build for yourself and the units you build to sell carry real costs too. In practice, these are the gaps.

Projects are tied to customers

In most ledgers a job or project hangs off a customer. A capital project you build for your own use, or homes and units you build to sell, have no customer, so their costs sit in general ledger accounts with nothing tracking them as a project.

Actuals, but no live budget or forecast

The books show what was spent. What each job should cost by cost code, revised by approved change orders, and what it will cost at completion usually live in a separate spreadsheet, so margin fade shows up after the job is done.

Change orders live in email

Few ledgers keep a change-order log that moves the contract value, the cost budget and the billing schedule together when a change is approved. Pending changes aren't visible at all.

No percentage-of-completion or WIP schedule

Earned revenue, over and under billings and loss provisions are rebuilt in a spreadsheet every month-end, from exports, for the bank, the bonding company and the auditor.

Holdback handled with workarounds

Progress billing against a schedule of values, with holdback retained and sales tax on the amount net of holdback, takes extra items, manual math and a separate receivable to track.

Labour reaches the job without its burden

CPP, EI, WSIB, EHT and benefits are real job costs, but they rarely make it onto the job. Labour looks cheaper than it is and every margin is overstated.

Uncoded costs quietly drop off the job

A bill entered without the right job, class or tracking category never appears in project reports, and nothing tells you it's missing.

Capital and inventory entries are booked by hand

Moving costs into construction in progress, capitalizing on the in-service date, moving work in process to finished goods and relieving cost of goods sold on sale all happen in spreadsheets and manual journal entries.

Job profit stops at gross margin

Rent, office salaries, trucks and insurance aren't in any job's profit, so the jobs that look profitable aren't always the ones that pay for the business.

How ProjectCost solves it

Your ledger stays the ledger. ProjectCost adds the project accounting on top.

Every gap above has the same root: the books record transactions, not projects. ProjectCost reads those transactions, assigns them to projects the way your books are already organized, and does the project accounting: budgets, forecasts, earned revenue, billing and the month-end entries.

Projects tied to customers

Cost-to-cost % complete, earned revenue, over and under billings and loss provisions, with the reversing entry drafted and each month's schedule saved as a snapshot.

Holdback workarounds

Progress billing with holdback built in

Schedule of values, previously billed, this period, holdback retained and tax on the net amount, with holdback receivable tracked on every job.

Labour without burden

Burdened labour on every hour

Hours from your ledger or field time app × pay rate × (1 + burden), with the burden entry drafted so the job carries the real cost.

Uncoded costs

Nothing falls through

Costs that don't match a project or cost code land in an Unassigned costs queue until someone codes them, with what the source said shown for context. Coding survives every re-import.

Manual capital & inventory entries

Entries drafted, balanced and tagged

Reclass to construction in progress or work in process, including labour. Capitalization in the in-service month. Units completed to finished goods and units sold to cost of goods sold, for any number of units.

Profit stops at gross

Profit after overhead

An overhead rate built from your Profit and Loss, applied on labour cost, labour hours or direct cost, your choice. A management view that never touches the WIP schedule.

What ProjectCost does not do

It doesn't replace your accounting system.
QuickBooks, Sage, Xero or whatever you use stays your general ledger. ProjectCost reads from it, connected or through exports, and drafts the entries for you to book there.
It isn't payroll or a time clock.
Hours come from your ledger or field time app, or are entered in ProjectCost; pay rates and burden are set per employee.
It doesn't judge your estimates.
Budgets, estimates to complete and contract values are management's. It applies them consistently and shows the consequences.
It isn't an estimating or scheduling tool.
It starts when the budget exists and follows the money from there.

How it works

Five steps, one afternoon.

It needs two things: your accounting data, connected or exported, and the budgets you already have for your projects. Everything else is import, calculation and review.

  1. 1

    Bring in your data

    Connect QuickBooks Online, or upload CSV and Excel exports from Sage, Xero, your field time app or your own workbooks. Columns are matched for you; you confirm before anything is saved.

  2. 2

    Load projects and budgets

    Projects, contract values and budgets by cost code, from a file or entered directly. Capital and build-for-sale projects included.

  3. 3

    Bring in costs and time

    Bills, expenses, journal lines and hours. Re-importing the same lines updates them instead of duplicating them.

  4. 4

    Code what's left

    Work through the Unassigned costs queue. Anything you code is kept on the next import or sync.

  5. 5

    Close the month

    Review the WIP schedule, book the drafted entries, save the snapshot. Every figure drills down to the transaction or spreadsheet row behind it.

A reasonable first run

  • Start with your three largest active jobs. They carry most of the margin risk, and their budgets usually exist already.
  • Run it at your last month-end. Compare the WIP schedule with the one you built by hand. Differences are worth understanding either way.
  • Clear Unassigned costs first. Costs that aren't on the right job are the most common reason a job looks better than it is.

Questions

Frequently asked questions

Which accounting systems does it work with?+

Any that can export to CSV or Excel: Sage 50, Sage 300, Xero, QuickBooks Desktop and others. QuickBooks Online can also be connected directly. Column names from Sage, Xero, QuickBooks Time, ClockShark and Procore exports are recognized automatically, and you can mix sources.

What can I import from spreadsheets?+

Projects, budgets, cost codes, cost transactions, time, employees and rates, invoices, change orders, the chart of accounts and a monthly Profit and Loss. Each has a template, and each upload shows a row-by-row preview before anything is saved.

What happens when I import the same costs again next month?+

They're updated, not duplicated, using your line ID or a fingerprint of the row. Costs you've already coded to a project keep that coding.

Does it write back to my accounting system?+

Not yet. It drafts journal entries with a [ProjectCost] memo for you to book. With QuickBooks connected, the memo stops the next sync from counting them twice.

How is sales tax handled?+

In Canada, recoverable GST/HST on purchases (input tax credits) is kept out of job cost. In the US, sales tax paid is part of the cost.

Can I trace a number back to its source?+

Yes. Cost to date, billed to date and each cost-code actual open the lines behind them: a link to the transaction in QuickBooks, or the spreadsheet file and row it came from.

What accounting basis does the WIP schedule use?+

Percentage of completion on a cost-to-cost basis, with projected losses recognized in full as soon as they're known, consistent with ASPE 3400 and IFRS 15.

Is my data separate from other companies'?+

Yes. Every record belongs to one company and the database itself refuses links between companies. Connection tokens are encrypted.

Who built it?+
